analysis.one_liner: Makes the 2001 and 2003 Bush tax cuts, including lower investment tax rates, permanent.
analysis.headline: The bill drew 146 cosponsors, all Republicans, but the House Ways and Means Committee never acted on it and it died without a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have erased the built-in expiration dates on the tax cuts passed in 2001 and 2003, making them permanent instead of ending between 2008 and 2010. That includes the lower top income tax rates, the repeal of the estate tax, and the low tax rates on capital gains and dividends. It would also permanently extend the deduction for state and local sales taxes, the tuition deduction, generous small-business equipment expensing, and the research tax credit. The bill was referred to the tax-writing committee and never moved.
analysis.who_benefits: High earners and investors gain the most, because the provisions that made the biggest difference after the 2001 law — the top income tax rate falling from 39.6% to 35%, the estate tax repeal, and the 15% capital gains and dividends rates — apply overwhelmingly to households with large incomes and investment holdings [S2] [S3]. Middle-income families also gain from the 10% bracket, the child tax credit, and marriage penalty relief made permanent [S2]. Small business owners gain from a permanently higher equipment expensing limit ($125,000 instead of $25,000), and companies that spend on research gain a permanent credit [S3]. Taxpayers in states with no income tax gain from the permanent sales tax deduction [S2] [S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: High earners, investors, and small businesses

how_it_helps.text: The bill repeals the December 31, 2010 termination date in the 2001 tax law, making every cut in that law permanent, including lower rates across all income brackets and the estate tax phase-out [S2] [S3].

It makes permanent the reduced income tax rates on dividends and capital gains enacted in 2003 — 15% instead of rates up to 35% — which primarily benefit households with large investment income [S2] [S3].

It permanently raises the small-business expensing allowance to $125,000 with a phase-out beginning at $500,000 in investment, letting businesses deduct equipment purchases immediately rather than over years [S3].
It makes the research and development tax credit permanent, eliminating its repeated short-term extensions, effective for amounts paid after December 31, 2007 [S3].
It permanently extends the deduction for state and local sales taxes and the deduction for tuition and related expenses [S2] [S3].

analysis.who_pays: The federal Treasury pays, because making the cuts permanent removes the revenue that would return when the expirations took effect, adding to deficits year after year rather than ending a temporary cost. Ordinary taxpayers ultimately bear that through future borrowing, interest costs, or later tax increases. Permanent estate tax repeal, in particular, concentrates its benefit on the wealthiest few thousand estates each year while costing tens of billions annually.

drawbacks.text: The bill makes the tax cuts permanent with no offsetting revenue, so the cost rolls into deficits indefinitely; the 2001 and 2003 laws were written with sunset dates in part because their long-term cost — on the order of trillions of dollars over a decade — was not fully paid for [S2].

The largest per-household gains go to the top of the income distribution: the estate tax repeal, the 35% top rate, and the 15% capital gains and dividends rates each concentrate their benefits on high-income households with large estates or investment income [S2] [S3].

The bill's only response to tax-code complexity is a nonbinding 'sense of the House' asking the Ways and Means Committee to report simplification legislation by the end of 2008 — a statement with no force of law [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill would deliver real tax cuts to most working families, but its design concentrates the largest and most permanent gains at the top and pays for none of it. Permanence is the expensive part: a temporary cut can lapse when its cost becomes unsustainable, but this bill would lock in roughly $2 trillion or more in revenue loss per decade, with the estate tax repeal alone among the costliest provisions and its benefits confined to the largest estates. A stronger bill would have made middle-class provisions permanent while leaving the top-rate, estate, and investment-tax cuts subject to review.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee the day it was introduced, the committee never took it up, and it sat there until the two-year Congress ended in January 2009 [S1] [S5].

narrative.text: Rep. Tim Walberg (R-MI) introduced the bill on June 14, 2007, with 146 Republican cosponsors and no Democratic cosponsors [S2] [S4].
The House referred it to the Ways and Means Committee the same day; no markup, vote, or further action ever appears in the record [S5].
Democrats controlled the House in the 110th Congress, and the Ways and Means chairman never scheduled the bill for consideration, so it died in committee without a floor vote [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died, the scheduled expirations of the 2001 and 2003 tax cuts stood, and the Treasury kept the revenue that permanence would have surrendered. High earners, large estates, and investors lost the chance at permanently lower rates; no one else materially gained.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Federal Treasury kept the scheduled revenue

for.name: Rep. Tim Walberg
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to make the 2001 and 2003 tax cuts permanent.

for.name: 146 of 202 House Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; every cosponsor listed was a Republican.

against.name: Rep. Charles Rangel
against.role: Chair, House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a markup or committee vote after its referral; the record shows no committee action.

against.name: Speaker Nancy Pelosi
against.what_they_did: Did not bring the bill to the House floor; with Democratic control of the chamber, no vote was ever scheduled.

sides.party_line_note: All 146 cosponsors were Republicans; the Democratic majority controlled the committee and the floor and never acted on the bill.

industries.note: Permanent 35% top rate and 15% capital gains and dividends rates deliver the largest dollar gains to households at the top, paid for with permanent revenue loss that the public ultimately bears through deficits.
Permanent repeal of the estate tax's scheduled return benefits only the biggest estates, which make up a small fraction of deaths, while costing the Treasury tens of billions a year.
A permanent $125,000 expensing allowance lets small firms deduct equipment immediately; the benefit flows to business owners but is broadly similar to what workers at those firms gain from growth.
A permanent research tax credit ends the uncertainty of repeated short-term extensions and lowers the after-tax cost of research spending; the credit also carries through to products consumers use.

industries.industry: Taxpayers in states without an income tax (e.g., Texas, Florida)
industries.note: The permanent sales tax deduction primarily helps residents of the handful of states that levy no state income tax; it has little effect elsewhere.
